title: Discovery That Sells
description: Go beyond surface-level questions and uncover the real motivations, fears, and needs driving every caller. Great discovery makes the appointment feel inevitable.

modules.title: The Iceberg Model
modules.objective: Understand what customers say vs. what they actually mean
modules.lesson:
The Iceberg Model

What a customer tells you on the phone is the tip of the iceberg. Beneath the surface: their timeline, their budget anxiety, their past bad experience at a dealership, their spouse's opinion, their fear of making the wrong choice. Discovery is about understanding the whole iceberg.

What They Say vs. What They Mean

"I'm just looking" → I'm genuinely interested but don't want to feel pressured
"What's your best price?" → I want to know if I can trust you
"I'm still comparing options" → I haven't found anyone I connect with yet
"I don't need anything fancy" → I have a budget I'm nervous to share

The Discovery Mindset

Stop thinking of discovery as information-gathering and start thinking of it as storytelling. You're inviting the customer to tell you their story. When they feel heard, they stop guarding and start sharing — and that's when the real conversation begins.

Never Assume

The customer asking about a $60k truck might be buying it for their business. The person asking about a base model might have $80k in the bank and just be frugal. Assume nothing. Ask everything.

Practice Goal

Ashley called about a specific model but you don't know why. Use discovery to uncover what's really driving her purchase — don't pitch until you understand her full situation.

modules.title: The Four Question Types
modules.objective: Use situational, problem, implication, and vision questions to build a full picture
modules.lesson:
The Four Question Types

Not all questions are equal. The best phone-up reps use a layered system that moves the customer from surface to depth — from "what they want" to "why they want it."

The Four Types

Situational: Establish the baseline. "What are you driving now?" "How long have you had it?"

Problem: Find the pain. "What's the main thing you're looking to improve or change?" "What's driving the timing right now?"

Implication: Deepen the pain. "How has that been affecting your daily commute?" "Is that creating any issues for your family?"

Vision: Get them selling themselves. "Ideally, what would a perfect vehicle look like for your life right now?" "If everything worked out perfectly, when would you want to be driving the new car?"

The Rule of 3

Never accept the first answer. The real reason someone is buying usually comes out in the third or fourth exchange. Keep asking follow-up questions before you recommend anything.

Practice Goal

Tyler is a first-time buyer. Use all four question types to understand his full situation before suggesting a single vehicle.

modules.title: Listening Between the Lines
modules.objective: Hear what the customer isn't saying and respond to it
modules.lesson:
Listening Between the Lines

The most underrated skill in phone sales isn't talking — it's listening. Not passive listening while you wait for your turn to speak, but active listening that catches hesitations, contradictions, and emotional signals buried in the words.

The Pause Signal

When a customer pauses before answering a question, that pause is data. It usually means: they're hiding something, they're uncertain, or they've hit on something emotionally loaded. Don't fill the silence — let it breathe, then gently ask: "What's your hesitation there?"

Mirror-Back Technique

Repeat their key words back to them:
Customer: "I just need something reliable."
You: "Something reliable — what's happened with your current car?"
This signals that you actually heard them and often unlocks a deeper story.

The Contradiction Tell

If someone says they're "not in a rush" but is calling on a Tuesday morning, that's a contradiction. Note it and gently probe: "You mentioned you're not in a rush — is there a timeframe we're working around at all?"

Practice Goal

James will tell you part of his story. Your job is to hear what he's not saying and draw out the full picture through careful listening and follow-up questions.

modules.title: Trade-In as a Discovery Tool
modules.objective: Use the trade-in conversation to uncover budget, timeline, and emotional context
modules.lesson:
Trade-In as a Discovery Tool

The trade-in question is one of the most valuable discovery questions you can ask — and most reps rush past it. "What are you driving now?" unlocks a rich vein of information: how long they've had the car, what it means to them, why they're ready to move on, and what they're expecting to get for it.

The Trade-In Discovery Stack

  1. "What are you driving now?"
  2. "How long have you had it?" (timeline signal)
  3. "What's been the main thing that's motivated you to look at something new?" (pain)
  4. "Have you had it appraised anywhere, or are you starting fresh?" (price sensitivity)
  5. "Is the trade-in a big factor in your decision, or more of a nice-to-have?" (priority)

The Emotional Layer

Customers often have a real emotional relationship with their trade. A car that's been in the family, a vehicle that's been through a hard year, a truck that represents a chapter of life. Acknowledging this emotional element builds deep rapport that no pricing conversation can replicate.

Practice Goal

Margaret has a car to trade. Use the trade-in discovery stack to understand her full situation — financial, emotional, and timeline.

modules.title: Discovery on the Fast Lane
modules.objective: Conduct meaningful discovery when a customer is impatient and wants fast answers
modules.lesson:
Discovery on the Fast Lane

Not every customer gives you time to build a discovery conversation. Some want fast answers and have no patience for what they perceive as stalling. You need discovery techniques that work at speed — that gather crucial information quickly, without the customer even realizing it's happening.

The One-Question Shortcut

When time is tight, one question does the most work:
"Quick question before I look that up — are you trying to get into something in the next few weeks, or is this more of a longer-horizon thing?"
The answer to this one question tells you urgency, budget readiness, and where they are in the decision process.

Embedded Discovery

Weave discovery into your answers:
"I can tell you about that Camry — are you replacing a vehicle or adding to the fleet?"
The customer hears an answer coming; they don't notice the question embedded before it.

The Fast Summary

Once you have enough: "Okay — so [their situation]. Based on that, here's what I'd actually point you to first..." Summarizing back shows you were listening and earns a few more seconds of attention.

Practice Goal

Nina moves fast. She'll ask pointed questions and expect you to keep up. Conduct compressed, embedded discovery while maintaining her pace.
